name: Bob Marley and the Wailers
hook: The Kingston group that Lee Perry stripped down and Chris Blackwell repackaged as a rock album, which is how reggae reached the rest of the world.
blurb: Bob Marley was born on 6 February 1945 in Nine Mile, a village in Saint Ann, Jamaica, and grew up partly in Trenchtown, a poor part of Kingston. In 1963 he formed the Wailers with Peter Tosh and Bunny Wailer, and their first single, 'Simmer Down', produced by Coxsone Dodd at Studio One with the Skatalites, was a ska hit in Jamaica. In 1970 the producer Lee 'Scratch' Perry recorded them for 'Soul Rebels' (recorded August to November 1970 at Randy's, released by Trojan) and its follow-up, with the Barrett brothers as the rhythm section: a bare, spare sound of guitar, bass, drums, organ and voice that is often counted as the group's best work. In 1972 Chris Blackwell of Island Records signed them. Before releasing 'Catch a Fire' (April 1973) he remixed the Kingston sessions at Basing Street in London, adding rock guitar by the American Wayne Perkins and keyboards by John Bundrick, thinning out the heavy bass and packaging it like a rock album so that it would sell to rock fans. It worked: that decision is widely credited with taking Marley to a white rock audience, and it is the clearest case on this map of a label reshaping a record's sound for a market. Eric Clapton's cover of 'I Shot the Sheriff' was an American number one in 1974. Marley was a Rastafarian, and his songs were about poverty, faith and political violence. In December 1976 he was shot at his home in Kingston and survived. At the One Love Peace Concert in 1978 the rival party leaders Michael Manley and Edward Seaga shook hands on stage. He died of cancer in Miami on 11 May 1981, aged 36. 'Legend' (1984) is the best-selling reggae album.
